title: Democrats Will Wield Enormous Power in Statehouses. What Will They Do?
summary: While attention has focused on the incoming Democratic Congress, the real change could happen in state capitals where Democrats will control a dozen new statehouse chambers.

During the 2026 campaign, the reporters visited almost all of the states where partisan control and legislative supermajorities were at stake.


Nov. 16, 2026


Updated 10:16 a.m. ET


The midterm tsunami that swept Democrats to power in Congress also gave them control of state capitals from Pennsylvania to Nevada where they will be able to wield power swiftly and consequentially, in ways that will impact lives almost immediately.


Democrats will control the governorship and both legislative houses in six new states — Arizona, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Michigan and Minnesota — and hold the majority in a dozen new statehouse chambers.


At least 530 legislative seats changed parties across the country, the[Democrats’ best showing](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/04/us/politics/state-legislatures-democrats-midterm-election.html) since the Watergate era and the biggest partisan swing since Republicans gained more than 700 seats and flipped 22 chambers in 2010.


“It is hard to overstate how massive of a political earthquake this was,” said State Representative Oscar De Los Santos, the incoming Arizona House speaker, who at age 33, wasn’t even alive the last time Arizona Democrats held the majority in any legislative chamber.


What comes next could be dramatic.


In Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Nevada, Democrats want to raise the minimum wage, strengthen unions and pass paid family leave. They will face minimal opposition from powerless Republicans in the minority.


In Georgia and Texas, where Democrats will unexpectedly occupy the governor’s office and control their state houses, Republicans still holding the state senates will face enormous pressure to finally expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. Wisconsin,[one of the few states outside the South](https://www.kff.org/medicaid/status-of-state-medicaid-expansion-decisions/) that has not expanded Medicaid, could do so quickly.
